title: High-throughput long-context streaming demo — API & Console walkthrough
action_items: Diego: run 1M TPS simulator on Helion sample workload by 2025-07-30
Lena: send pricing for dedicated 4-GPU pool and burst options by 2025-07-24
Priya: provide sample 120k-token dataset link by 2025-07-25
summary: Redwood AE/SE walk Helion through a targeted demo of handling very long context windows (50k-120k tokens), high TPS scenarios (bursty up to ~1M TPS simulated), and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Key outcomes: validated caching and chunking approaches, discussed dedicated capacity + fallback routing, agreed next steps for POC and benchmarks.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Sarah Kim (Helion CTO), Tom Nguyen (Helion Platform Eng), Priya Desai (Helion ML Eng)

[00:00] Lena (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — we got Sarah, Tom, Priya?
[00:03] Sarah: yep hi, thanks for doing this, lena. we wanted to see how Redwood behaves when we push a lot of context and also heavy request rates — two pain points for us.
[00:09] Lena: perfect. diego will drive the demo, i'll chime on product/pricing. diego over to you.
[00:15] Diego (SE): cool, thanks. i'm going to share my screen — it's the console, plus a small benchmark harness. objective is threefold: one, long context (50k to 120k tokens) for our genomic notes; two, sustained and bursty TPS up to the tens/hundreds of thousands; three, streaming behavior — backpressure, partial responses, and client timeouts.
[00:29] [00:30] Tom: just to be explicit, our current setup is a k8s cluster with a small batching proxy; we do about 10k reqs/s normally but during digestion jobs it spikes much higher. we also need streaming for progressive decoding to UI.
[00:40] Diego: understood. i'll start with the API path for hosted, then show dedicated capacity config and the private deployment notes. first quick caveat — long contexts are handled two ways at runtime: prefix/KV caching when you have repeated prefixes, and chunking with retrieval-based assembly when you can't keep all kv in memory. i'll demo both.
[00:58] [01:00] Diego (sharing): ok sending first request — 60k token context, single concurrent request. console shows model selection (redwood/w-custom-70b, quantized), kernel profile auto-chosen: large-seq-optimized. response time is long as expected but stable — ~12s to first token because of KV warming.
[01:22] Priya: wait, 12 seconds to first token seems high. we need sub-2s for UI flows.
[01:27] Diego: yeah for UI you want prefix+streaming where the initial prompt is small and only later append long context; for monolithic 60k you won't get 2s. that's when we recommend either summarized index or external retrieval then streaming.
[01:40] Sarah: can you show the prefix caching? that's our main pattern — we preface prompts with patient canonical sections that repeat.
[01:46] Diego: on it — i'm toggling prefix cache in the route config. sending same request but with the first 6k tokens pinned as cached prefix. console shows cache hit: 93% KV hit, first token lat ~600ms.
[01:59] [02:00] Diego: note: hit rates depend on tokenization alignment — sometimes our auto-detect mislabels a section because of punctuation; it's not perfect.
[02:07] Tom: what about memory? if we keep big kv caches across many sessions won't we OOM?
[02:12] Diego: that's why dedicated capacity can be configured with per-route cache quotas and eviction policies. for hosted we expose cache size vs cost tradeoffs. also we have a rolling spill-to-disk option for private deployments.
[02:24] [02:30] Diego: moving to throughput tests — i'm going to ramp concurrent requests. harness simulates JWT-auth traffic with our SDK. first ramp to 20k rps sustained with small prompts (2-3 tokens input, streaming output).
[02:44] [02:45] Priya: are these token-output heavy? our typical flow is short prompt, 200 tokens out per response.
[02:50] Diego: yes similar. starting ramp — console shows per-instance qps, avg latency ~45ms, p95 ~120ms, token throughput 18k tps per GPU equivalent. autoscaler behavior: we have configured burst buckets so we can absorb short spikes without immediate spin-up.
[03:12] [03:15] Sarah: what's the graceful degradation if we hit a hard cap? do you return 503s or degrade model?
[03:20] Diego: configurable. default policy is above threshold we signal to routing to fall back to compatible cheaper variants or lower-context versions, and then 429s for rate-limited clients depending on SLA. in enterprise plans you can opt for queuing vs immediate failure.
[03:33] Tom: show the streaming backpressure scenario — e.g., clients that have slow TCP read or an intermittent mobile connection.
[03:38] Diego: good one. i'm going to simulate a slow consumer by artificially delaying the read loop. watch the stream in the console trace.
[03:44] [04:00] Diego (action): starting slow-consumer test. as responses start streaming, we see server-side send buffer increase; the runtime switches to backpressure mode: it reduces batch sizes, evicts some prefix KV writes to reduce memory, and signals the orchestration to reroute new requests away from that instance.
[04:20] Priya: does that mean in the UI we might see partial content and then a hang? user experience wise we need progressive partial updates.
[04:26] Diego: you'll get partial content. Redwood supports chunked streaming with explicit chunk indices so client can resume or drop incomplete chunks. we also expose per-stream timeout and keepalive settings at the SDK level.
[04:36] [04:45] Sarah: and if client times out and retries, do you charge double tokens?
[04:49] Diego: we have idempotency tokens so if a retry is detected within TTL and the original stream completed server-side, the retry will fetch cached output, avoiding double charge in many cases. If retry triggers re-execution because cache wasn't available, then yes you'll pay for re-generation. we recommended idempotency for mobile apps.
[05:04] [05:15] Priya: ok demo looks good. can we stress test with bursty traffic — like, sudden 200k rps for 30s? that's our worst-case on payroll ingestion.
[05:20] Diego: i can run a simulated burst but full 200k requires cluster-level quota we don't have in demo account; i'll simulate 60k burst and show how routing and fallback work.
[05:30] [05:45] Diego (running): ramping to 60k — watch the routing pane: fast autoscale triggers, dedicated pool increases instances, fallback model variant (w-custom-35b-quant) is enabled for non-critical routes. latency spikes then settles as new instances come up.
[05:55] Tom: you mentioned burst credits — is that the same as a reservoir token-bucket?
[06:00] Diego: yes it's a configured burst reservoir. you can set per-customer or per-route burst tokens and refill policies; useful for short digestion spikes.
[06:10] [06:30] Sarah: what about timeouts at the proxy level — our infra times out after 10s, but some of these long contexts need more.
[06:36] Diego: we recommend streaming first token fast using prefix+cache or a two-phase UX: quick summary first (sub-2s) then full assembly streamed in background. If you need >10s, you can extend proxy timeouts for dedicated routes and use background callbacks/webhooks for completion. 
[06:55] Priya: are webhooks retried if client doesn't acknowledge?
[06:58] Diego: yes, webhook delivery has exponential backoff and a DLQ option to inspect failed deliveries.
[07:06] [07:20] Lena: on the billing side — long contexts that force re-generation vs cached replies affect unit economics. our Console shows token-level cost and attribution so you can see per-request delta. would you like me to attach a sample cost spreadsheet?
[07:33] Sarah: yes please. also we need encryption at rest and KMS integration for private deployments. any limits there?
[07:40] Lena: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private, and for Dedicated you can opt-in on an account basis. audit logs are available for all enterprise tiers.
[07:50] Tom: back to performance — can you show traces for a request that had partial streaming and a retry?
[07:54] Diego (shares trace): here's a trace: notice the stall at 3.2s when the consumer paused; you can see batch shrink, queue time increases, and a fallback route decision at 6.1s. trace links to the token-level cost breakdown and to the console logs showing which kernel path was chosen.
[08:18] [08:30] Priya: the kernel path selection — is it deterministic? sometimes we've seen dev environments pick slower kernels.
[08:36] Diego: it's heuristics-based: model attention pattern, sequence length histogram, and hardware topology decide kernel selection. you can pin kernels in Private for determinism but hosted uses auto-select to optimize global efficiency.
[08:50] Sarah: what about model quantization and quality regressions? we don't want hallucinations to increase.
[08:55] Diego: Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workload; we run eval suites on your prompts to measure regression and can gate rollouts with canary checks. we've got a sample eval run in the demo repo.
[09:10] [09:30] Tom: what about losing partial state if an instance crashes mid-stream? do you reconstruct KV cache?
[09:36] Diego: KV cache is ephemeral in-memory by default; for critical flows we suggest prefix caching with external snapshot to object store or using Dedicated with redundant replicas. Private can enable persistent spill.
[09:48] Priya: any limits on maximum context? we have sequences that can be >150k tokens once expanded.
[09:54] Diego: currently practical limits depend on model architecture and deployment — we support up to ~200k in private with chunking+retrieval, but you should plan on retrieval + assembly for >120k to keep latency reasonable. we'll map specifics in POC.
[10:10] [10:20] Sarah: let's talk SLOs — we want 99.9% availability and p95 latency <200ms for short prompts.
[10:26] Lena: for short prompts on Dedicated that's achievable; we'll propose an SLA and an incident playbook. For hosted, p95 depends on region and model choice; we can show historic dashboards.
[10:36] [10:45] Diego: quick note on SDKs — we expose a client keepalive and adaptive concurrency control. SDK logs will auto-surface slow consumers so you can monitor client-side too.
[10:55] Priya: could you push the simulated slow consumer logs to our Slack channel? that would help the infra team.
[11:00] Lena: sure — we'll share the console trace link and a short packet capture gist.
[11:06] [11:15] Diego: wrapping up, i'm starting a final run that combines 60k burst and some 60k tokens contexts on background jobs to show mixed workload behavior. console shows isolation — background long-context jobs are routed to a heavy-mem dedicated pool while interactive short prompts use a low-latency pool.
[11:30] Tom: nice. do you provide tooling to pre-calculate expected token cost per job?
[11:34] Diego: yes, cost estimator in Redwood Optimize plus a CLI tool that simulates tokenization and estimates token inflation for your dataset.
[11:42] Sarah: ok let's recap next steps.
[11:46] Lena: recap — we will: 1) send the long-context performance spreadsheet and a recommended dedicated config (Lena); 2) Diego will run the 1M-TPS simulator on Helion workload sample and share results (Diego); 3) Helion to provide 120k-token sample dataset and internal SSO/infra contact (Priya/Tom). propose POC kickoff Aug 4.
[11:59] Priya: sounds good. also want the private deployment checklist — compliance folks will need that.
[12:04] Lena: will include.
[12:08] Sarah: thanks everyone, this was useful — we have a better sense of trade-offs.
[12:11] Lena: thanks all. we'll follow up with links in the next 24 hours.

Transcript notes: transcription has minor errors (proper nouns sometimes off), occasional speaker mislabels. references: console trace link: https://redwood.example/trace/ff-20250722-7d3c (demo-only link), demo repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/demo-long-context (redacted), cost spreadsheet attachment promised.

End of transcript.
